content.chapter: Chapter 1 — Al-Andalus and a Great Traveler
objectives: Say where and when Al-Andalus was (parts of Spain and Portugal, 711–1492).
Describe how Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side in Al-Andalus.
Look at irregular past forms (built, took, brought, had) and at because / because of / so.
Describe a city with one fact, one reason and one result.
content.pedagogy: Start with a map of the Mediterranean: Spain in the west, Mecca in the east. The chapter is a short history page, so learners build a fact card for four cities (Valencia, Granada, Sevilla, Córdoba) and check every number in the text. Grammar grows out of the same sentences: “Is this now or in the past? What is the verb today?” and “Is there a noun or a full sentence after because?”
priorKnowledge: Past forms with -ed and big numbers (700,000; 1,000).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Al-Andalus is not a city; it is the name of the land Muslims ruled in parts of Spain and Portugal.
Ibn Jubayr was born in Valencia, not in Granada; he later worked in Granada (Chapter 2).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: irregular past forms (built, took, brought, had) · because + sentence · because of + noun · so + result.
Notice (Activity 1): write “They built one of the greatest cultures of the Middle Ages in the West.” on the board and ask: “Is this now or in the past? What is the verb today?” Learners match build → built, take → took, bring → brought, have → had.
Build (Activity 2): “Al-Andalus was in Europe because of its location …” / “Córdoba had 700,000 people, so it was the largest city …” / “This great culture surprised the people of that time because Muslims lived a much better life than them.” Ask: “Noun or sentence after the gap? Reason or result?”
Likely errors: *because its location · *buyed / *bringed · *taked.
Use (Activity 3): three sentences about a big city with a fact, because of and so.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: al-AN-da-lus, va-LEN-ci-a, gra-NA-da, se-VIL-ya, COR-do-ba.
Numbers: “seven hundred thousand”, “seven eleven to fourteen ninety-two”.
Weak because: /bɪkəz/. Irregular past: brought /brɔːt/, took /tʊk/, built /bɪlt/.
beforeReading: Show a map with Spain and Mecca. Ask: “How can a traveler go from Spain to Mecca 800 years ago?” Pairs guess (by sea? by land?) and keep their guesses for Chapter 4.
duringReading: First listening: Which cities do you hear?
Read and make a fact card for each city (born here / bigger than … / 500 bathhouses / 700,000 people).
Underline the three groups who lived side by side.
Circle because, because of and so.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the fact cards in view.
Language Focus: Past forms (Activity 1), because / because of / so (Activity 2), describe a city (Activity 3).
Write two sentences: One fact about Al-Andalus and one about Ibn Jubayr.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Map hook: Spain and Mecca, pairs guess how people travelled; 5–12 Listen with books closed (which cities?), then read along; 12–19 City fact cards in pairs, whole-class check with “Where does it say that?”; 19–23 Quick Challenge individually; 23–31 Language Focus Activities 1–2 as discovery (past or now? noun or sentence?); 31–38 Activity 3: pairs describe a city in three sentences, two volunteers speak; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Muslims, Christians and Jews often do together in Al-Andalus?
Why did the great culture surprise people of that time?
Which city was the largest in Western Europe? Why?
interactiveTips: Use the “Living Side by Side” hotspot before reading paragraph 1 aloud.
Use the “A City Rich in Learning” hotspot to fix the year 1145 and Valencia.
Replay paragraph 4 when learners mix up the cities.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give four city cards and four fact strips to match before writing. Let learners copy built, took and brought from the text first.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing two cities of Al-Andalus with bigger, largest, because of and so, using only facts from the chapter.

formativeAssessment: Matches each city with its fact from the text.
Chooses because of + noun and because + sentence.
expectedResponses: Ibn Jubayr was born in Valencia in 1145. In Al-Andalus, Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side. Córdoba had 700,000 people, so it was the largest city in Western Europe.
content.transferTask: Describe a big city you know in three sentences with because of and so.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners check every number against the text, and did they notice the difference between because and because of themselves?

exitTicket: Complete: “In Al-Andalus, Muslims, Christians and Jews ____. Córdoba was the largest city because ____.”

content.chapter: Chapter 2 — A Young Scholar from Granada
objectives: Compare Ibn Jubayr with Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta (when they traveled and how far).
Describe Ibn Jubayr’s education and job before the journey.
Name three goals of his journey (Hajj, new knowledge and skills, information about other Muslim lands).
Use when + past for a time and dream / want / goal + to + verb.
Talk about their own dreams in three sentences.
content.pedagogy: Draw a simple life line: young → grew up → 1183. Learners place facts from the text on it. Then a “goals” box: They find three goals and notice that each one has to + verb. The grammar is discovered from the chapter sentences before the rule is named.
priorKnowledge: Want to + verb in the present (I want to …).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Ibn Jubayr traveled less than Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta, but he traveled first and wrote one of the first travel books.
He did not visit Baghdad or Damascus before 1183; the chapter lists cities he visited on his journey.
He was not young when the journey started: He was middle-aged.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: When + past sentence for a time · dream / want / goal + to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): “When he was young, Ibn Jubayr studied hard …” / “When he grew up, he got a job …” Ask: “Does When give a time, a reason or a place?”
Build (Activity 2): “One of his biggest dreams was to go on Hajj. He also wanted to gain … Another goal … was to get information …” Ask: “What comes after was and wanted here?”
Likely errors: *wanted gain · *dream was go · *When he young.
Use (Activity 3): “One of my biggest dreams is to … I also want to … Another goal is to …”
content.pronunciationFocus:
Linking: “wanted to” /ˈwɒntɪd tə/, “to go” with weak to /tə/.
Word focus: GAIN new KNOWL-edge /ˈnɒlɪdʒ/ (silent k), SEC-re-tar-y, GOV-er-nor.
Cities: BAGH-dad, MO-sul, A-lep-po, je-RU-sa-lem, da-MAS-cus.
beforeReading: Ask: “What was your biggest dream when you were small?” Two or three learners answer with one word; write the words on the board.
duringReading: First listening: Which two other travelers do you hear? How far did each one go?
What was his biggest dream?
Read and complete the life line (young / grew up / 1183).
Find three goals of the trip and underline to + verb.
Circle the five Eastern cities.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: When … (Activity 1), dreams and goals with to + verb (Activity 2), my biggest dream (Activity 3).
Write one sentence about Ibn Jubayr’s job.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Dream hook; 4–11 Listen for the biggest dream, then read; 11–18 Life line and goals box in pairs, check with the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 30–38 Activity 3 in pairs, then write the three sentences; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Ibn Jubayr traveled less than Ibn Battuta. Why is he still important?
What did Ibn Jubayr study when he was young?
What job did he have in Granada?
Why did he want to visit other Muslim lands?
interactiveTips: Use the “A Good Education” hotspot to collect the three subjects.
Use the “Work in Granada” hotspot for secretary and governor.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “When he was young, he ____. When he grew up, he ____. His dream was to ____.” with a word bank.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about a person in their family: When he/she was young, his/her job, and one dream with to + verb.

formativeAssessment: Places education, job and journey in the right order.
Uses to + verb after dream, want and goal.
expectedResponses: When he was young, Ibn Jubayr studied Islam, languages and literature. He worked as a secretary for the governor of Granada. One of his biggest dreams was to go on Hajj.
content.transferTask: Say three sentences about your own dreams and goals with to + verb.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover to + verb from the three goal sentences before I named it?

exitTicket: Complete: “When he grew up, Ibn Jubayr ____. One of his dreams was ____.”

content.chapter: Chapter 3 — The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
objectives: Explain what the Rihla is and why it made Ibn Jubayr famous.
Say why the journey was long and dangerous at the end of the twelfth century.
Notice almost (= nearly) and use by + transport / on foot.
Say how they travelled on a real trip.
content.pedagogy: Bring a real notebook into class and write today’s date and one sentence in it: “This is a diary.” Learners then read to find out what Ibn Jubayr wrote in his diary and why it became a model. A two-column chart (What he wrote about / Why the journey was hard) organises the reading.
priorKnowledge: Transport words: boat, ship, camel, bus, car.
The idea of a diary or a notebook.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Rihla is the name of his book; rihla means “travel book” in Arabic.
He did not write years later: He wrote almost every day while he still remembered the details.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: almost (= nearly) · by + transport / on foot.
Notice (Activity 1): “Ibn Jubayr wrote down everything he saw and heard almost every day …” Ask: “Every single day, or nearly every day?” Then compare “Almost the whole area was a war zone.”
Build (Activity 2): “He traveled [by] boat, by camel, and [on] foot to visit Mecca.” Ask: “Why is walking different?”
Likely errors: *by foot · *with boat · *by a camel.
Use (Activity 3): “Last …, I traveled to … by … . Then we went to … on foot.”
content.pronunciationFocus:
Word focus: TRIP, TRAV-el DI-a-ry, de-SCRIBES, SIGHTS /saɪts/, cru-SA-ders, PRIS-on-ers, SLAVES, WAR zone, med-i-ter-RA-ne-an.
Rihla: RIH-la. Chunk: “by BOAT, | by CAM-el, | and on FOOT”.
beforeReading: Show a notebook and ask: “What do people write in a diary?” Collect three ideas.
duringReading: First listening: What is the name of his book?
Fill the two-column chart: What he wrote about / why the journey was hard.
Find how long the journey took.
Underline the three ways he travelled.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Almost (Activity 1), by / on (Activity 2), how did you travel? (Activity 3).
Write one diary sentence about today.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Diary hook; 5–12 Listen for the book’s name, then read; 12–19 Two-column chart in pairs; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–30 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 30–38 Activity 3: pairs tell a real trip, then write one diary sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the word rihla mean?
Why did his book become a model?
How long did the journey take, and how did he travel?
interactiveTips: Use the “A Travel Diary” hotspot before the second paragraph.
Use the “By Boat, Camel and Foot” hotspot to check the three ways of travelling.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a picture card for each way of travelling (boat, camel, walking) and the frames “by ____ / on ____”.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a four-sentence diary entry about a real day with almost, by and on foot.

formativeAssessment: Gives one reason the journey was hard.
Uses by + transport and on foot correctly.
expectedResponses: His book is the Rihla. It means travel book. He wrote almost every day. He traveled by boat, by camel and on foot.
content.transferTask: Write one diary sentence about a real trip with by or on foot.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the chart to separate what he wrote about from why the journey was hard?

exitTicket: Complete: “The Rihla is ____. He wrote almost ____.”

objectives: Follow the route from Granada to Ceuta, across the sea, to Alexandria and on to Cairo.
Say why Ibn Jubayr chose the sea route.
Notice while + was/were + -ing for a longer action, and use While / After / Then / finally.
Retell a route in order.
content.pedagogy: Learners trace the route on a simple Mediterranean outline with their finger as they listen: Granada, Ceuta, Sardinia, Sicily, Crete, Alexandria. Each stop gets one fact. The order words in the chapter are the grammar target, so the route itself becomes the practice.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of common verbs (went, took, arrived).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Christian soldiers in Alexandria were prisoners. An army from Cairo stopped them one day away from Medina.
The storm came between Sardinia and Sicily, not near Alexandria.
The lighthouse was more than 50 men tall; this is a comparison, not 50 floors.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: while + was/were + -ing (longer action) · After / Then / finally for order.
Notice (Activity 1): “While they were sailing between these islands, a terrible storm caught them.” Ask: “Which action was already happening? Which one came in the middle?”
Build (Activity 2): complete While / After / Then / finally in the route sentences.
Likely errors: *While they sailed, a storm was catching · *Finally it arrive.
Use (Activity 3): retell the route, then the learner’s own route to school.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Places: SEU-ta, sar-DIN-i-a, SIC-i-ly, CRETE, al-ex-AN-dri-a, CAI-ro.
Date: “February the third, eleven eighty-three”.
Word focus: ROUTE /ruːt/, LIGHT-house, a-MAZED /əˈmeɪzd/.
beforeReading: Look back at the Chapter 1 guesses: by sea or by land? Learners predict which one Ibn Jubayr chose.
duringReading: First listening: Trace the route with a finger on the map.
Write one fact for each stop.
Find the sentence that compares sea and land travel.
Find what he saw near Sardinia and when he got off the ship in Alexandria.
Find what amazed him in Alexandria.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (sequencing).
Language Focus: While (Activity 1), order words (Activity 2), retell the route (Activity 3).
Write the route in four sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Prediction check; 4–12 Listen and trace the route, then read; 12–18 One fact per stop in pairs; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 30–38 Activity 3: retell in pairs, then own route to school; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Ibn Jubayr travel by sea?
What happened between Sardinia and Sicily?
Who were the prisoners in Alexandria, and who stopped them?
What did he write about the lighthouse?
interactiveTips: Use the “A Terrible Storm” hotspot when the storm sentence is read.
Use the “A Famous Lighthouse” hotspot for the size of the lighthouse.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the route as five picture cards to order, with the frames “First …, Then …, Finally …”.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the route as a diary entry from Ibn Jubayr (“On February 3, I left Granada …”) with while and after.

formativeAssessment: Gives the reason for the sea route.
Uses while + was/were + -ing and order words.
expectedResponses: First, he went to Ceuta. Then he took a Genoese ship. While they were sailing, a storm caught them. Finally, he arrived in Alexandria.
content.transferTask: Tell your route from home to school with First, Then and Finally.
content.teacherReflection: Did tracing the route on the map help learners keep the order without reading every line again?

objectives: Describe what Ibn Jubayr saw in Cairo: the walls, the bridge, the free hospital, the pyramids and the Nilometer.
Explain why he respected Saladin, using examples from the text.
Notice so + adjective + that and use did not / could + base verb and used it to + verb.
Describe a good leader with examples.
content.pedagogy: This is a long, fact-rich chapter, so groups of three each take one paragraph and become “experts”, then teach the class with one sentence and one number. A class “Saladin did …” chart collects examples of kindness, generosity and fair rules: Every example must point to a sentence.
priorKnowledge: Places in a city: hospital, school, mosque, bridge.
Did not + verb in the past.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The hospital was completely free, and it had separate areas for men, women and patients who needed special care.
The bridge was high because of the yearly floods, not for ships.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: so + adjective + that (result) · did not / could + base verb · used it to + verb (purpose).
Notice (Activity 1): “The roads were also so safe that people could travel day and night without any fear.” Ask: “How safe? What was the result?”
Build (Activity 2): “Saladin did not ask …”, “People used it to measure …”, “people could travel …”.
Likely errors: *did not asked · *used it for measure · *could to travel.
Use (Activity 3): describe a good leader with gives support to …, does not …, so … that ….
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: sa-LAH ad-DIN al-ay-YU-bi, SAL-a-din, ay-YU-bid.
Word focus: PRAISED, MOSQUE /mɒsk/, FEAR, NO-ticed, EN-e-my at-TACKS, un-der con-STRUC-tion, FLOODS /flʌdz/, SEP-a-rate /ˈsepərət/, PYR-a-mids, MEAS-ure /ˈmeʒər/, GUEST-hous-es, NI-lom-e-ter.
Numbers: “two thousand loaves”, “eight thousand to ten thousand”.
beforeReading: Write “A good ruler …” on the board. Pairs add two actions. Keep them to compare with Saladin.
duringReading: First listening: Which places in Cairo do you hear?
Expert groups: One paragraph each, one sentence and one number to teach.
Build the “Saladin did …” chart.
Find why the bridge was high.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: So … that (Activity 1), did not / used it to / could (Activity 2), a good leader (Activity 3).
Compare the board list with Saladin’s actions.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Good-ruler hook; 4–11 Listen for places, then read; 11–20 Expert groups and teaching round; 20–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 31–38 Activity 3 in pairs; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Ibn Jubayr feel great respect for Saladin?
What was special about the hospital?
What did Saladin build for students, teachers and poor people?
interactiveTips: Use the “A High Bridge” hotspot with the floods sentence.
Use the “The Nilometer” hotspot to explain what a tool to measure means.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a picture list (bridge, walls, hospital, bread, pyramids) to tick while listening, then the frame “He saw ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about Saladin’s Cairo, each with a number or a reason from the text.

formativeAssessment: Gives two examples of Saladin’s kindness or fair rules from the text.
Explains the bridge and the Nilometer.
Uses did not / could + base verb.
expectedResponses: Saladin gave support to mosques, hospitals and schools. He did not ask the farmers to pay the Nile water taxes. The roads were so safe that people could travel day and night.
content.transferTask: Describe a good leader for a school or a town in three sentences.
content.teacherReflection: Did every example on the Saladin chart come with a sentence from the text?

exitTicket: Complete: “Saladin did not ____. The hospital was ____.”

objectives: Describe a camel caravan and how you could see who was rich and who was poor.
Notice be like + noun for comparing two things.
Use who, needed to + verb and plural were.
Describe a picture with “It is like …”.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is short and visual, so the lesson centres on the picture. Learners first describe what they see, then read and compare: What does the text say about the tents? The comparison “like beautiful moving palaces” becomes the language model.
priorKnowledge: Animal and desert words: camel, sand, desert.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The tents were not real palaces; they were like palaces.
The caravan went to the Red Sea, on the way to Mecca.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be like + noun · who for people · needed to + verb · plural + were.
Notice (Activity 1): “They were like beautiful moving palaces.” Ask: “Were they palaces?”
Build (Activity 2): “… who was rich and who was poor … You only needed to look … The tents … were amazing.”
Likely errors: *were like beautiful (no noun) · *The tents was.
Use (Activity 3): describe the chapter picture with is like / are like.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Word focus: CAR-a-van, TENTS, ROY-al /ˈrɔɪəl/, MOV-ing PAL-a-ces.
Weak were in “They were like” /ðeɪ wə laɪk/.
beforeReading: Show only the picture. Pairs say three things they see.
duringReading: First listening: How could you see who was rich?
Read and underline the comparison with like.
Find where the caravan was going.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Be like (Activity 1), rich and poor (Activity 2), describe the picture (Activity 3).
Draw a small tent and write one sentence with is like.
content.lessonPlan: 0–6 Picture talk; 6–12 Listen and read; 12–17 Comparison hunt; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 29–38 Activity 3 and a short drawing with a sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Where was the caravan going?
What were the tents of rich royal people like?
Why do you think travelers joined a caravan?
interactiveTips: Use the “Moving Palaces” hotspot on the red tent.
Use the “A Long Line of Camels” hotspot for the word caravan.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “The ____ is like ____.” with picture word cards.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences comparing a rich traveler and a poor traveler in the caravan, using only the text.

formativeAssessment: Explains how to see rich and poor in a caravan.
expectedResponses: You could see who was rich and who was poor. You only needed to look at their tents. The tents of royal people were like moving palaces.
content.transferTask: Describe a photo from your own life with It is like … .
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the picture to support their understanding of the comparison?

objectives: Say when Ibn Jubayr arrived in Mecca and how long he stayed.
Explain his comparison of Mecca with a mother’s body.
Notice can / cannot for possible and not possible, and use with respect and such as.
Describe a special place with “is located in” and “can”.
content.pedagogy: The chapter quotes Ibn Jubayr directly. Read the quote slowly and let learners picture it: A narrow valley that gets bigger for a very big crowd. Learners explain the comparison in their own words before the grammar step. Treat the Ka’bah and the Great Mosque with respect; no role play of worship.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Mecca is like a mother's body” is a comparison: The valley makes space for the crowd, as a mother's body makes space for her baby.
He stayed more than eight months, not eight days.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: can / cannot + base verb · with respect (how) · such as (examples) · is located in.
Notice (Activity 1): “… it can get bigger and have space for a very big crowd of people.” / “… that city cannot hold them.” Ask: “Possible or not possible?”
Build (Activity 2): complete with respect, such as and surprisingly.
Likely errors: *can to hold · *such as Persia and India and Africa are (no verb).
Use (Activity 3): describe a special place with is located in, can, and with respect or such as.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Word focus: NAR-row, MIR-a-cles, GI-ant /ˈdʒaɪənt/, CROWD /kraʊd/, with re-SPECT.
Ka’bah: KA‘-bah. Weak can /kən/ vs strong can’t / cannot.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can one place hold millions of people?” Learners guess in one sentence.
duringReading: First listening: When did he arrive, and how long did he stay?
Read the quote and draw a quick sketch: Narrow valley, huge crowd.
Underline can and cannot.
Find the countries people came from.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: can / cannot (Activity 1), with respect and such as (Activity 2), a special place (Activity 3).
Write the comparison in your own words.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Guessing hook; 4–11 Listen for date and length, then read; 11–17 Sketch and explain the comparison; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 29–38 Activity 3 in pairs; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does Ibn Jubayr compare Mecca to a mother’s body?
Where did the people in Mecca come from?
How does he describe the Great Mosque?
interactiveTips: Use the “The Holy Ka’bah” hotspot with the words with respect.
Use the “Hills around Mecca” hotspot to show the narrow valley.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “Mecca is in a ____ valley. It can hold ____.” with a word bank.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write three sentences explaining the comparison, with can, cannot and however.

formativeAssessment: Uses with respect or such as.
expectedResponses: Mecca is in a narrow valley, but it can have space for a very big crowd. A mother’s body makes space for her baby. The biggest city on earth cannot hold this crowd.
content.transferTask: Describe a place that is special to you with is located in and can.
content.teacherReflection: Did the sketch help learners understand the comparison before they read the grammar?

exitTicket: Complete: “Mecca is located in ____. It can ____.”

objectives: Follow the route from Medina through the desert to Baghdad.
Describe Baghdad at that time (Abbasid capital, 2,000 bathhouses, eleven Friday mosques).
Use to / through / near / for and was / were / stayed.
Describe their own town with there is / there are.
content.pedagogy: Continue the route map from Chapter 4. Learners add Medina, the desert, the Euphrates and Baghdad, with one fact each. The prepositions of movement are taught with arrows on the map: To (arrow to a place), through (arrow across), near (arrow beside).
anticipatedMisconceptions: He saw Baghdad about 75 years before the Mongol attack, not after it.
He stayed in Medina only five nights.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to / through / near / for · was (one) / were (many) · stayed.
Notice (Activity 1): match he went to Medina, through the desert, near the Euphrates River, for only five nights.
Build (Activity 2): “Baghdad was …”, “there were 2,000 bathhouses …”, “stayed there for only five nights”.
Likely errors: *there was 2,000 bathhouses · *in the desert (when through is meant).
Use (Activity 3): “In my town, there are … There is a … near …”
content.pronunciationFocus:
Places: me-DI-na, eu-PHRA-tes, AB-ba-sids, MON-gols.
Numbers: “two thousand”, “eleven”, “seventy-five years”, “twelve fifty-eight”.
Word focus: DES-ert (noun), NORTH-EAST.
beforeReading: On the route map, ask: “What is between Medina and Baghdad?” (the desert).
duringReading: First listening: How many nights in Medina?
Add four stops to the route map with arrows.
Find two numbers about Baghdad.
Find the year of the Mongol attack.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Words for moving (Activity 1), was / were (Activity 2), in my town (Activity 3).
Write one sentence about Baghdad with there were.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Map question; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–17 Route arrows in pairs; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus Activities 1–2; 29–38 Activity 3 written and shared; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How did he travel from Medina to Baghdad?
What was Baghdad at that time?
Why is his description of Baghdad important?
interactiveTips: Use the “The Abbasid Capital” hotspot with the numbers.
Use the “Near a Great River” hotspot to show near.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give arrow cards (to, through, near) to place on the map before writing.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short route description from Medina to northern Syria with four prepositions.

formativeAssessment: Uses there were with plural numbers.
expectedResponses: He stayed in Medina for only five nights. He traveled through the desert to Baghdad. Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasids. There were 2,000 bathhouses there.
content.transferTask: Write three sentences about your town with there is / there are and near.
content.teacherReflection: Did the arrows on the map make the prepositions clear without long explanations?

exitTicket: Complete: “He traveled through ____. In Baghdad, there were ____.”

content.chapter: Chapter 9 — Damascus and Its Great Mosque
objectives: List parts of the Great Mosque of Damascus that Ibn Jubayr describes.
Explain why his description is useful today (before 1401 and 1893).
Notice present simple for what a book says; use helped / could + base verb.
Describe a building with a list.
content.pedagogy: Learners make a “mosque parts” word web from the long list in paragraph 1, then match parts to the picture. metadata.title: Ibn Jubayr A2 — Teacher Guide
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, grammar learners discover from the story, and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 13 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow short supported narrative and historical texts and give short spoken or written answers with frames and oral rehearsal.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 listening, reading, speaking and writing through the journey of Ibn Jubayr, a great Andalusian traveler of the Middle Ages, from Al-Andalus to Mecca and back, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading come first: learners find the meaning and the evidence in the text, and the Quick Challenge checks understanding. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence and answer a simple meaning question (Is this now or past? Possible or not possible? Advice or rule?), so they find the rule themselves before it is confirmed; then they PRACTISE it in short, controlled tasks; finally they USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own life. A simple route map, built chapter by chapter, keeps the journey clear. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: Thirteen Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Evidence checks (fact cards, route map, charts, storyboards)
Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: A short, chapter-specific start: a map, a picture, a prediction or one question about the learners’ own life.
readingFramework.during: Listen first with one simple question, then read and do one concrete evidence task (fact cards, route map, chart, storyboard).
readingFramework.after: Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (Look → Practise → Use), then short production about the learners’ own world and an exit ticket.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise the chapter Word Notes and the words needed for the chapter task.
vocabularyApproach.method: Guess the meaning from the sentence, the picture or the audio before any explanation; check stress aloud.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse the words in the Use task, the exit ticket and the whole-book review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask one simple meaning question, let learners say the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. At A2, keep metalanguage to a minimum and use examples instead of terms. The explanation in the app appears only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: irregular past (built, took, brought, had); because / because of / so
Ch2: When + past; dream / want / goal + to + verb
Ch3: almost; by + transport / on foot
Ch4: while + was/were + -ing; After / Then / finally
Ch5: so + adjective + that; did not / could + base verb; used it to + verb
Ch6: be like + noun; who; needed to; plural were
Ch7: can / cannot; with respect; such as; is located in
Ch8: to / through / near / for; was / were
Ch9: present simple for what a book says; could + base verb
Ch10: about / nearly / in / later; to + verb for purpose
Ch11: almost + past verb; In + year / Then / In the end
Ch12: had to + base verb; have to / should for tips
Ch13: should; told … to; just as … as; could not; wiser

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find explicit evidence, follow a route, order events and compare facts.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: listen for one simple question first, then replay short parts for detail.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: give short supported retells, descriptions and advice after pair rehearsal.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write three to five short connected sentences with the chapter’s language about the learners’ own life.

valuesFocus: D1 Justice — Saladin’s fair rules and support for people in need
D9 Compassion — free hospitals, bread for the poor and help for travelers
D12 Patience — a journey of two years and three and a half months, waiting for good winds
D14 Respect — Muslims, Christians and Jews living side by side; describing holy places respectfully
D16 Responsibility — writing down details carefully and sharing knowledge
D20 Helpfulness — King William II helping the passengers; gifts for students and travelers
languageFocus: Every one of the 13 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (three activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask one simple meaning question before naming the form.
Let learners answer first; the explanation after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At A2 the Use step is short spoken or written production about the learners’ own world, rehearsed in pairs first.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Support with picture cards, sentence strips, word banks, strong frames, the route map and audio replay; let learners copy forms from the text before writing their own. Extend with one or two more sentences or a clearly labelled personal example, never with facts from outside the book.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Religious words and phrases (Hajj, the Ka’bah, “Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)”, hadiths) are read and explained respectfully; they are never gapped, corrected or rewritten.
Do not role-play worship, war, robbery or shipwreck scenes; describe them and discuss what the text says.
Keep personal application separate from facts about Ibn Jubayr.
Do not add dates, places or events that are not in this A2 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Ibn Jubayr’s journey crosses Europe, Africa and Asia. It shows how travel, trade and learning connected people of different faiths and cultures, and how a traveler can learn from every place.

themes.title: Living side by side:
themes.description: In Al-Andalus, Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side and often worked, traded and studied together (Chapter 1).

themes.title: Help for travelers and students:
themes.description: Colleges, guesthouses and gifts of money helped students, teachers and travelers in Egypt and Damascus (Chapters 5 and 9).

themes.title: Help across faiths:
themes.description: A Christian king, William II, helped the Muslim and Christian passengers after the shipwreck (Chapter 11).

themes.title: Learning through travel:
themes.description: Ibn Jubayr told young people to travel and look for knowledge (Chapter 13).

actions: Make a class “welcome” card in English for a new student or a visitor.
Make a simple travel map of a real or planned class trip with one fact for each stop.
Interview a family member about a journey they made and write three sentences.

miniProject.title: Our Travel Diary
miniProject.desc: In groups, make a small illustrated travel diary in English for a real or planned trip (a school trip, a family visit). Each page has a date, a place, how you traveled, one thing you saw and one thing you learned. Use the book’s language: “On …, we traveled to … by …”, “We stayed there for …”, “It was bigger than …”, “That’s why …”. Add one sentence from the book exactly as it is.

reflectivePrompt.title: What a Journey Teaches
reflectivePrompt.desc: Ibn Jubayr said his journey made him a wiser person. Write four to six sentences about a trip that taught you something. Where did you go? What did you see? What did you learn?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D1 Justice / D9 Compassion

metadata.title: Ibn Jubayr A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Look • Listen • Read • Check • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who study the story of the traveler Ibn Jubayr at home or on their own.
learningGoals: Understand the 13 chapters of Ibn Jubayr’s journey.
Follow his route from Al-Andalus to Mecca and back.
Find the answer sentence in the story.
Learn the Word Notes of each chapter.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen or read first, then check.
Answer the Quick Challenge before you read the feedback.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter at a Time
sections.text: Study one chapter in one sitting. It takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” to see the steps for your chapter.
points: Look at the title and the picture.
Listen and follow the text.
Read one paragraph at a time.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Listen first when audio is available, then read.
points: First time: Listen or read for the main idea.
Second time: Follow the words with your eyes.
Stop and say one short sentence again.

sections.title: 3. Follow the Route
sections.text: Ibn Jubayr traveled from Granada to Mecca and back. Keep a small route list in your notebook.
points: Write each new place.
Add one fact for each place.
Use the route to retell the story.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has underlined words. Tap a word to see its Word Note. Tap the two hotspots on the picture for short notes.
points: Read the word in its sentence first.
Guess the meaning, then check the Word Note.
Write the word and one sentence in your notebook.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has one Quick Challenge and three Language Focus activities.
points: Answer first, then read the feedback.
Wrong answer? Find the answer sentence and try again.
Activity 1: look. Activity 2: practise. Activity 3: use the language about your own life.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and numbers. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Write the names and numbers in a list.
Look at the picture and the hotspots again.
Learn only two words today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: Ibn Jubayr’s journey shows respect, patience, helpfulness and love of learning. Turn each value into one small action.
points: Respect: Different people lived side by side (Chapter 1).
Kindness and fairness: Saladin helped poor and sick people (Chapter 5).
Patience: He waited for good winds (Chapter 10).
Helpfulness: A king helped the passengers (Chapter 11).
Learning: Travel and look for knowledge (Chapter 13).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge
